summary: A 1970 note discussing a possible protocol plateau, a point at which the protocols might be considered stable enough to build on. It is a discussion piece by Jon Postel and Steve Crocker.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 48 reviews open design questions for the early Network Control Program. Postel and Crocker recommend some approaches, explain unresolved issues, and emphasize that their implementation sketch is not mandatory.

questions: what is the network control program
how should the ncp handle errors
what is a possible protocol plateau
subtitle: A 1970 discussion of design choices for the Network Control Program.

tldr.problem: Early NCP design raised questions about message padding, reconnection, errors, status testing, layering, and room for experimentation.
tldr.mechanism: Postel and Crocker review these questions and state preferences, including using marking rather than double padding, treating reconnection as optional, and reserving link numbers for experiments.
tldr.outcome: RFC 48 presents recommendations and an illustrative NCP structure; it says its implementation material is not binding.

today: RFC 48 is an early discussion of NCP design choices. Its implementation material is illustrative, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: Padding, Reconnection, and Links
sections.content:
The authors discuss ways to align messages to machine word boundaries. They suggest using marking to adjust message length rather than double padding, while noting that they have no strong preference because their hosts can send word fragments.

They also discuss dynamic reconnection. They say it should not be required in the initial protocol and propose offering it later as an optional experimental tool. For simplicity, they recommend keeping links coupled to connections rather than adding destination sockets to message text.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors favor marking over double padding, but do not make that choice a requirement. They recommend keeping reconnection optional and keeping links tied to connections for simplicity.

sections.title: Errors and Status Testing
sections.content:
The authors distinguish resource overload from other errors. They say flow control should handle overload, while error generation should be optional and errors should be recorded in chronological files locally and at the receiver.

For debugging, they suggest a distinct link such as link 255 for status requests and replies. They also describe an echo command pair: an NCP receiving ECO would reply with ERP.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal uses flow control for overload and local logs for errors. It also reserves a way to request status and test whether another NCP responds.

sections.title: Layers and Experimentation
sections.content:
The authors identify three levels: the IMP network protocol, the NCP protocol at the host level, and user or subsystem protocols above it. They want the NCP to remain simple and neutral, leaving login and other user-level behavior above it.

They recommend assigning link numbers 2 through 31 to regular connections and 32 through 255 for experiments. They also recommend reserving control-command prefixes from 255 downward for experimentation.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal separates the IMP, NCP, and user-protocol roles. It also sets aside link numbers and command prefixes for experiments.

sections.title: An Illustrative NCP Structure
sections.content:
The RFC sketches a possible NCP environment with processes, ports, sockets, and event channels. It lists sample system calls such as Init, Listen, Close, Transmit, and Status.

Its NCP sketch has input and output handlers, interpreters, a scheduler, and tables for rendezvous and links. The authors state that these assumptions and implementation choices are descriptive only and do not constrain the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The final sections show one possible way to organize NCP software. Sites can use different local designs.
